newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU reach meat deal, but fail on poultry.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU reach meat deal, but fail on poultry.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials averted a potentially costly trans-Altantic trade war on Wednesday when they at least partially settled a long fight over meat import regulations, a senior U.S. Agriculture Department official announced.

The agreement did not resolve sharp disagreements in poultry issues. U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek said about $50 million worth of U.S. poultry exports to Europe would remain halted and announced that up to $1 million worth of European poultry products would no longer be accepted into the United States.
The agreement, such as it was, however, gave negotiators a way out of what could have been a very ugly situation.
The so-called veterinary equivalency agreement enabled Washington to cancel plans at the last minute to remove more than 100 European meat plants from its list of approved exporters.

The move would have blocked the flow of around $300 million worth of European meat products to the United States, mostly pork products from Denmark and Italian hams, and would likely have escalated the trade fight even further.

U.S. officials praised the deal -- which was reached just hours before a midnight deadline -- and said it would expand U.S. meat exports to Europe, with pork likely to benefit most in the near term. They said it also maintained bilateral trade worth some $3 billion in pet food, dairy and egg products.
"We think this is a good agreement for us ... It's not a perfect agreement," said U.S. negotiator Drazek.
U.S. poultry groups harshly criticised the pact as an action that will "slam the door shut" for imports of U.S. poultry.

"The unreasonable and unyielding stance of the European Union during trade talks is nothing more than a blatant attempt to restrict competition from U.S. poultry companies in Europe," said a statement issued by the National Broiler Council, the National Turkey Federation and the USA Poultry and Egg Export Council.
The U.S. poultry industry stands to lose $34.2 million in broiler trade with the EU, plus $10 million in turkeys and $8 million in spent hens, the groups said.
Drazek said European and U.S. officials were unable to reach agreement on methods the U.S. poultry industry uses to decontaminate carcasses, and its use of a chlorine solution to kill bacteria.

He said Washington and Brussels will continue to try to work out the remaining issues, but sources did not expect success any time soon. Negotiators have struggled for three years to reach even a partial accord in the difficult talks.

In the meantime, Drazek also announced that European poultry exports to the United States would stop because of health safety concerns. He said this would impact mostly chicken pate imports from France, worth about $1 million.
New rules implemented by the EU on April 1 have already halted U.S. poultry shipments to European destinations.
The agreement, which will go into effect October 1, could increase U.S. meat exports because of changes Europe agreed to in approving U.S. pork and beef plants for exports.
Currently only eight U.S. pork plants and two beef plants can sell to Europe, but the agreement will allow many more plants to export once they are approved by U.S. inspectors.
Meat industry officials applauded the hard-fought deal.
"This is a significant win for U.S. beef producers," said Max Deets, president of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association and a beef producer from Beloit, Kansas.

The United States currently ships only small amounts of pork to Europe and no beef. Europe has long banned imports of hormone-treated beef. The hormone issue is currently being discussed at the World Trade Organisation in Geneva, and meat industry sources said they hoped that Wednesday's deal would open the door to successful resolution of the hormone dispute.
